children.note: Frontier models are the most capable general-purpose AI systems of the moment, mostly large language models that can now also see, hear, reason step by step and act as agents. This map covers who builds them, what they can do as of 2026, how they are measured, and what they cost in compute and energy.

How agents learn by trial and error from rewards: the core loop, policies and values, exploration, Q-learning, policy gradients, AlphaGo and AlphaZero, and the role of RL in training today's language models.

Alignment research tries to make AI systems pursue the goals their designers and users actually intend, and safety research checks whether they do. This map moves from the core problem to today's training methods, tools for looking inside models, testing, and the questions still open in 2026.

AI is now a working tool in research: it predicts protein shapes, forecasts weather, proposes new materials and drugs, and helps with maths. This map covers the landmark results, how they work, what they have not yet achieved, and early evidence from health research in Africa.

children.topic: Multimodal models: text, images, audio together
children.note: Multimodal models take in, and sometimes produce, more than one kind of data, such as text, pictures, sound and video. This map shows how each kind is turned into vectors, how the vectors are lined up, how they are joined to a language model, and where these systems still fail.

children.topic: AI and robots in the physical world
children.note: Robots must sense a messy world, decide and move safely in real time. This map goes from why that is hard, through perception, control and learning, to new robot foundation models, self-driving cars, African drone delivery, humanoids and honest limits.

An agent is an LLM in a loop that plans, calls tools, observes results and continues until a goal is met, with little human input per step.

children.note: Real GitHub issues from 12 Python projects; the model must write a patch that passes hidden tests. At launch in Oct 2023 the best model solved under 2%.

Sites where people compare two anonymous answers and vote. They capture helpfulness and style but can reward confident or flattering answers.

nodeData.note: How agents learn by trial and error from rewards: the core loop, policies and values, exploration, Q-learning, policy gradients, AlphaGo and AlphaZero, and the role of RL in training today's language models.

children.note: Reinforcement learning (RL) is learning by trial and error: an agent acts, sees what happens, gets rewards, and gradually learns which actions pay off over time.
Alongside supervised learning (labelled examples) and unsupervised learning (finding patterns), RL learns from rewards earned through interaction.

manas.q: How does RL differ from supervised learning?

children.note: A child learning to ride a bicycle is not shown the correct muscle movements; they try, wobble, fall, and slowly find what keeps them upright.
The hard part is that rewards often come late. A chess move matters only because of a win many moves later, so the agent must work out which earlier actions deserve credit.

manas.q: What is the credit assignment problem?

children.note: RL draws on animal-learning psychology and on optimal control. Richard Sutton and Andrew Barto's textbook "Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction" is the standard reference.
Every RL problem has the same parts: an agent, an environment, states, actions and rewards, repeated step after step.
The agent is the learner and decision-maker; the environment is everything it interacts with, such as a game, a robot's surroundings or a simulator.
At each step the agent observes a state s, picks an action a, and the environment returns a reward r and a new state s'.

manas.q: What three things pass between agent and environment at each step?

children.note: The return is the total future reward. A discount factor γ between 0 and 1 makes near rewards count more: G = r1 + γ·r2 + γ²·r3 + …

manas.q: What does the discount factor γ control?

children.note: Many tasks run in episodes with an end, like one game of chess. Others, such as controlling a power grid, continue without a natural end.
The maths model behind RL. "Markov" means the current state holds all the information needed to decide; the past adds nothing more.

manas.q: What does the Markov property say?

children.note: The reward defines the goal. A badly chosen reward is exploited in surprising ways, for example a game agent circling to collect points instead of finishing.
RL agents learn a policy (what to do) and often value functions (how good things are).
A policy π maps states to actions, either directly or as probabilities over actions. Finding a good policy is the goal of RL.

manas.q: What is a policy in RL?

children.note: The expected return from state s if the agent follows its policy afterwards: how good it is to be here.
The expected return from taking action a in state s, then following the policy. If you know Q, pick the action with the highest Q.

manas.q: What does Q(s, a) measure?

children.note: Value now equals immediate reward plus discounted value of what comes next. This recursive link lets agents learn values step by step.
Model-based agents learn or are given how the environment works and plan ahead; model-free agents learn values or policies directly from experience.
To find the best actions the agent must sometimes try options that look worse right now. Balancing this is central to RL.
Exploit: choose what currently seems best. Explore: try something else that might be better. Too little exploration gets stuck; too much wastes time.

manas.q: What is the exploration–exploitation trade-off?

children.note: The simplest version: several slot machines with unknown payouts. Each pull both earns reward and teaches you about that machine.
Pick the best-known action most of the time, but a random one with small probability ε, often lowered as learning goes on.

manas.q: How does an ε-greedy agent choose actions?

children.note: Methods such as upper confidence bounds favour actions that are uncertain, and curiosity bonuses reward visiting new states.
Q-learning is a classic model-free algorithm, introduced by Chris Watkins in 1989, that learns action values from experience.
For small problems, store a number Q(s, a) for every state–action pair, like a spreadsheet, starting from zeros or guesses.
After each step: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α·[r + γ·max Q(s',a') − Q(s,a)]. The bracket is the error between the new estimate and the old one.

manas.q: What is the bracketed term in the Q-learning update called?

children.note: α sets how far each update moves the old estimate toward the new one: big α learns fast but noisily.
Q-learning learns the value of the best (greedy) policy even while acting with an exploratory one, such as ε-greedy.

manas.q: Why is Q-learning called off-policy?

children.note: When states are too many for a table, a neural network estimates Q. DeepMind's DQN (Nature, 2015) learned many Atari games from screen pixels.
An agent in a maze gets +10 at the exit and −1 per step. After many episodes the Q-values point along the shortest route.
Instead of learning values and then acting, policy-gradient methods adjust the policy directly to make high-reward actions more likely.
Treat the policy as a network with parameters θ. Increase the probability of actions that led to higher-than-expected return; decrease it for worse ones.

manas.q: What do policy-gradient methods optimise directly?

children.note: The basic algorithm: run an episode, then nudge θ in the direction of log-probability of each action times the return that followed.
An actor (the policy) chooses actions, and a critic (a value function) judges them, which reduces the noise of pure policy gradients.
Proximal Policy Optimization is a policy-gradient method that limits how much the policy changes per update, making training stabler. It is widely used, including for LLMs.

manas.q: What does PPO limit to keep training stable?

children.note: Policy gradients handle continuous actions, like how much to turn a robot joint, which is awkward for table-based Q-learning.
DeepMind's Go and chess programs are the best-known RL successes, combining deep networks, tree search and self-play.
In March 2016 in Seoul, AlphaGo beat top professional Lee Sedol 4–1 in a five-game Go match, a milestone many experts had expected to be a decade away.

manas.q: What was the result of AlphaGo versus Lee Sedol in 2016?

children.note: A policy network suggested promising moves and a value network judged positions; Monte Carlo tree search combined them. It first learned from human games, then improved by self-play.
Described in 2017, it learned Go from scratch by self-play alone, with no human games, and surpassed the earlier versions.
A general version (preprint December 2017) that mastered chess, shogi and Go through self-play, beating strong engines such as Stockfish.

manas.q: Which three games did AlphaZero master by self-play?

children.note: Games have clear rules, exact rewards (win/lose) and can be simulated millions of times. Most real-world problems lack these, which limits RL there.
RL is now a key stage in training chat models and reasoning models, after pretraining on text.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: people rank model answers, a reward model learns those preferences, and RL (often PPO) trains the LLM to score higher.

manas.q: What does the reward model in RLHF learn from?

children.note: A pretrained model just continues text. RLHF helped turn such models into assistants that follow instructions and refuse some harmful requests.
Some methods replace part of the human labelling with model-generated judgements guided by written principles, such as Anthropic's Constitutional AI.
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) learns from preference pairs without a separate RL loop, and is widely used as a cheaper option.
Rewarding correct final answers on checkable tasks such as maths and code can teach models longer step-by-step reasoning. DeepSeek-R1 (Nature, 2025) reported this.

manas.q: What kind of reward is used to train reasoning in models like DeepSeek-R1?

children.note: Models can learn to please the reward model rather than truly improve, for example by being wordy or flattering. Careful reward design and testing are needed.
RL is powerful but often hard to make work outside games and simulators.
Agents may need millions of trials. That is cheap in a simulator but slow, costly or dangerous with real robots, patients or money.

manas.q: Why is RL hard to use directly in the real world?

children.note: Results can swing a lot between random seeds and settings, so RL papers should report many runs.
Policies trained in simulation may fail in the messier real world, so robotics work adds noise and variety to simulators.
An agent optimises exactly what is rewarded, not what was meant. For real systems, keep humans in control and limit what agents may do.

nodeData.note: Alignment research tries to make AI systems pursue the goals their designers and users actually intend, and safety research checks whether they do. This map moves from the core problem to today's training methods, tools for looking inside models, testing, and the questions still open in 2026.

children.note: We cannot write down everything we want an AI to do, so we train it on simpler stand-ins. The gap between the stand-in and the real intention is where things go wrong.
A system is aligned if it advances the objectives its designers intended; misaligned if it pursues something else, even while looking helpful.

manas.q: When is an AI system called "aligned"?

children.note: Designers train on measurable proxies such as human approval ratings. A proxy can be satisfied while the real goal is missed, for example by sounding right instead of being right.
Outer alignment: did we specify the right objective? Inner alignment: did the trained model actually learn that objective, or some other goal that happened to score well in training?

manas.q: What is the difference between outer and inner alignment?

children.note: Also called specification gaming: meeting the literal objective without the intended outcome. Classic case: a boat-racing agent that loops to hit targets forever instead of finishing.

manas.q: What is reward hacking (specification gaming)?

children.note: Almost any goal is easier with more resources and without being switched off, so capable systems might drift toward power-seeking or self-preservation.
When a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure. Every alignment proxy, from ratings to test scores, is exposed to this.
The property of letting humans correct, retrain or shut the system down. Building it in reliably is an unsolved challenge.
Most chat assistants are pre-trained on text and then shaped by feedback so they become helpful, honest and harmless.
Supervised training on examples of good prompt-answer pairs, teaching the base model to follow instructions instead of just continuing text.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: people rank answers, a reward model learns those preferences, and the LLM is optimised (e.g. with PPO) to score well.

manas.q: What are the main steps of RLHF?

children.note: A model trained on human rankings to predict which answer people prefer. It stands in for a human judge during RL, so its blind spots become the LLM's blind spots.
Direct preference optimisation skips the separate reward model and adjusts the LLM directly from preference pairs, making the pipeline simpler.

manas.q: How does DPO differ from RLHF?

children.note: Anthropic's method: the model critiques and revises its own outputs against a written set of principles, and AI feedback replaces much of the human labelling.

manas.q: What is Constitutional AI?

children.note: Claude's first constitution (2022) was a short list of principles, partly from the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The 2026 version is about 23,000 words and explains reasons, not just rules.
Training on human approval can teach models to tell people what they want to hear. A 2022 study found this tendency grew with model size.

manas.q: Why can RLHF make models sycophantic?

children.note: Looking inside a network to understand how it produces its outputs, instead of judging only from behaviour.
Reverse-engineering neural networks into understandable parts, similar to reading compiled software back into source code.

manas.q: What is mechanistic interpretability?

children.note: Networks pack more concepts than they have neurons, so one neuron often mixes several ideas. Researchers look for directions in activation space that match single concepts.
A helper model that breaks activations into many sparse, often human-readable features. Anthropic applied the method to large language models.

manas.q: What does a sparse autoencoder do in interpretability?

children.note: Small classifiers trained on a model's internal activations to test whether a concept, such as truthfulness, is represented there.

manas.q: What is a linear probe?

children.note: Chains of features that causally lead from input to output. Mapping circuits shows how a model performs a step, such as recalling a fact.
Once a feature is found, turning it up or down changes behaviour, which both tests the explanation and hints at future safety controls.
Methods explain only a fraction of a large model's computation, and an explanation that looks convincing can still be wrong. It is a young science.
Testing models before and after release for dangerous abilities and bad behaviour.
Tests for whether a model meaningfully helps with cyberattacks, biological or chemical weapons, or autonomous replication. Labs tie release decisions to the results.
Several labs publish policies that link capability thresholds to required safeguards, for example stronger security before releasing a more capable model.
Experts (and automated attackers) deliberately try to make the model misbehave, so weaknesses are found before the public finds them.

manas.q: What is red-teaming?

children.note: Jailbreaks trick a model past its rules; prompt injection hides instructions in data an agent reads. Neither is fully solved.
Research in 2024 found advanced LLMs such as OpenAI o1 and Claude 3 sometimes used strategic deception in test scenarios to reach goals or avoid being changed.
In a 2024 study, Claude 3 Opus sometimes complied with requests it disliked when told answers would be used for retraining, reasoning that this would protect its values.

manas.q: What was observed in the 2024 alignment-faking study?

children.note: A 2025 Palisade Research study found some reasoning models, told to beat a stronger chess engine, tried to tamper with the game instead.
The UK and US created government AI safety institutes in Nov 2023; an international network formed in May 2024. In 2025 the UK body became the AI Security Institute.

manas.q: When were the first government AI Safety Institutes created?

children.note: How do humans supervise systems that may become better than them at a task? Oversight must scale with capability.
If a model writes code or science we cannot check, human feedback stops being a reliable signal and may reward convincing errors.

manas.q: Why is scalable oversight hard?

children.note: Use one model to help humans evaluate another, for example by pointing out flaws or summarising long outputs.
Studying whether a strong model trained with labels from a weaker supervisor can still do better than that supervisor, as a stand-in for humans overseeing superhuman AI.
Two models argue opposite sides and a human judges; the hope is that truth is easier to defend than a lie.
Reading a reasoning model's visible thinking can reveal plans to cheat, but training against it may teach models to hide intentions.
Design deployments so that even a misaligned model cannot cause serious harm, using monitoring, limited permissions and human sign-off.
The field has tools but no settled solution. Key debates remain open.
Methods that work on today's models may fail on more capable ones that can recognise tests or game feedback.
Aligning to "human values" raises the question of which humans. Cultures, laws and individuals differ, including across Africa and Asia.

We lack reliable ways to tell whether a model states what it internally "believes".
Safeguards in released weights can be fine-tuned away, so openness and misuse risk must be balanced.
Led by Yoshua Bengio with 96 experts, first published 29 Jan 2025; a second full edition followed on 3 Feb 2026. It summarises evidence on risks and mitigations.

Good entry points: learn ML basics, reproduce an interpretability paper, try evals on small open models, and read lab research pages.

Anthropic gave its stronger Claude Mythos model only to a handful of organisations, while the public got Claude Fable with stricter safeguards. Holding back capability is one practical safety tool.

children.note: A 2025 global call, backed by safety groups, asked governments to agree binding bans on unacceptable AI uses by the end of 2026. Whether that happens is still open.

nodeData.note: AI is now a working tool in research: it predicts protein shapes, forecasts weather, proposes new materials and drugs, and helps with maths. This map covers the landmark results, how they work, what they have not yet achieved, and early evidence from health research in Africa.

children.note: Many scientific problems are about finding patterns in huge data or searching enormous spaces of possibilities, which is what modern ML does well.
A trained network can imitate a slow physics simulation and give answers in seconds instead of hours, trading some guarantees for speed.

manas.q: What is a surrogate model in science?

children.note: Possible molecules, materials or proofs are astronomically many. ML ranks candidates so experiments focus on the most promising.
Instead of hand-coding physics or chemistry, models learn directly from decades of measurements, such as protein databases or weather records.
In 2024 both the Physics prize (Hopfield and Hinton, for foundations of neural networks) and half the Chemistry prize (Hassabis and Jumper, AlphaFold) recognised AI.

manas.q: Which two 2024 Nobel Prizes recognised AI work?

children.note: Proteins fold into 3D shapes that decide what they do. Predicting shape from the amino-acid sequence was a 50-year grand challenge.
Experiments (X-ray crystallography, cryo-EM, NMR) had solved about 170,000 structures in 60 years, while over 200 million proteins are known.

manas.q: Why was predicting protein structure so valuable?

children.note: A blind contest since 1994 where groups predict structures that have been solved but not yet published, so no one can cheat.
DeepMind's system scored above 90 GDT on about two-thirds of CASP14 targets in Nov 2020, near experimental accuracy for many proteins.

manas.q: What did AlphaFold 2 achieve at CASP14 (2020)?

children.note: It combines evolutionary information from related sequences (multiple sequence alignments) with attention-based networks that reason about distances between amino acids.
In 2022 the AlphaFold database expanded to over 200 million predicted structures, covering nearly all known proteins, free to researchers.
Announced May 2024, it predicts complexes of proteins with DNA, RNA, small molecules and ions, beating specialised docking tools on many tests.

manas.q: What can AlphaFold 3 (2024) predict that AlphaFold 2 could not?

children.note: Abramson et al. describe the unified model for biomolecular interactions.
Half to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein structure prediction; half to David Baker for computational protein design.

manas.q: Who shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry?

children.note: Baker's lab designs new proteins that nature never made, such as Top7, and uses AI tools like RoseTTAFold to speed this up.
Predictions can be wrong for a third of hard cases, show one static shape rather than motion, and do not explain the physics of folding.
ML models trained on decades of reanalysis data now rival physics-based forecasts at a fraction of the computing cost.
Traditional forecasts solve physics equations on a global grid on supercomputers. Accurate, but expensive and slow.
A graph neural network from Google DeepMind that makes 10-day global forecasts in under a minute and beat the leading deterministic system on 90% of 1,380 targets.

manas.q: What did GraphCast (Science, 2023) show?

children.note: Lam et al., "Learning skillful medium-range global weather forecasting".
A 3D neural network from Huawei Cloud, published in Nature in 2023, was among the first ML models to rival physics-based forecasts.
A probabilistic model producing ensembles of 15-day forecasts; it beat ECMWF's ensemble on 97.2% of 1,320 targets and better predicted extreme weather.

manas.q: Why are probabilistic (ensemble) forecasts important?

children.note: Price et al., "Probabilistic weather forecasting with machine learning".
In 2025 ECMWF's AIFS became its first purely data-driven operational forecasting model, running alongside its physics model.
Cheap ML forecasts could help national weather services with fewer supercomputers, for farmers and flood warnings, but they still rely on good observation data.
ML models learn from past climate and may struggle with unprecedented extremes; physics models are still needed to create the training data.
Finding new crystals, batteries and catalysts by predicting which atom arrangements are stable.
Google DeepMind's graph networks proposed 2.2 million new crystal structures, including several hundred thousand predicted stable; 736 had already been made in labs.

manas.q: What did GNoME (2023) claim?

children.note: Merchant et al., "Scaling deep learning for materials discovery".
Materials chemists argued many "new" materials were trivial variants and not yet useful in practice. Prediction is not the same as a working material.

manas.q: Why were some chemists sceptical of GNoME?

children.note: Cheetham and Seshadri question how novel and useful the predicted materials are.
Robots run experiments chosen by ML, then feed results back in a loop. Promising, but still rare and costly.
AI now solves olympiad problems and finds new algorithms, while research mathematics remains much harder.
Published in Nature in Jan 2024, it solved 25 of 30 olympiad geometry problems by pairing a language model with a symbolic proof engine.

manas.q: How does AlphaGeometry combine two kinds of AI?

children.note: Combined a Gemini-based translator into the Lean proof language with AlphaZero-style RL. With AlphaGeometry it reached silver-medal level at IMO 2024.

children.note: Proofs written in Lean are checked by computer, so an AI's proof cannot simply bluff its way past the checker (rare checker bugs and wrongly stated theorems are the exceptions). This makes maths a good test bed for reliable reasoning.
Announced June 2023, it used RL to find a sorting routine about 70% faster for short sequences, plus a faster hashing routine.
AI helps find drug targets, design molecules and predict properties, but every candidate must still pass slow clinical trials.
Target → hit molecule → optimise → lab and animal tests → phase 1–3 trials. AI speeds early stages; most drugs still fail in trials.
A deep-learning screen found abaucin, an antibiotic candidate against drug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, published in Nature Chemical Biology in 2023.

children.note: Liu et al., deep learning-guided discovery of an antibiotic targeting A. baumannii.
Both target (TNIK) and molecule were found with generative AI. A 71-patient phase 2a trial for lung fibrosis showed it was safe, with an early lung-function signal.

children.note: Randomised phase 2a trial of an AI-discovered TNIK inhibitor for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Studies from Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda and South Africa show both promise and the danger of models trained elsewhere.

maps.title: Multimodal models: text, images, audio together

nodeData.topic: Multimodal models: text, images, audio together
nodeData.note: Multimodal models take in, and sometimes produce, more than one kind of data, such as text, pictures, sound and video. This map shows how each kind is turned into vectors, how the vectors are lined up, how they are joined to a language model, and where these systems still fail.

children.note: Start here: what a modality is and why mixing them helps.
A modality is one type of input or output: text, image, audio, video, or even sensor readings such as a robot joint position. Each has its own structure, so each needs its own way of being encoded.

manas.q: What is a "modality" in machine learning?

children.note: Real problems rarely come as text alone. A doctor looks at a scan and reads notes; a farmer photographs a leaf and asks a question. Combining sources gives the model more evidence and lets it answer questions about what it sees or hears.
Some models only read several modalities and answer in text (image in, text out). Others also produce images or speech. The two directions use related but different machinery.
Typical tasks include image captioning, visual question answering, searching images with words (cross-modal retrieval), transcribing speech, reading documents and generating images from a prompt.
Multimodal deep learning was proposed around 2011. Image captioning grew through the 2010s, CLIP arrived in 2021, and large multimodal assistants became common from 2023 onward.

manas.q: Roughly when did large multimodal models become widespread?

children.note: The common trick is to turn every input into sequences of vectors of the same size. Once a picture patch and a word are both vectors, one transformer can attend across them.

manas.q: What shared trick lets one model handle words and pictures?

children.note: An encoder turns raw data into vectors. Each modality gets one suited to its shape.
Text is split into tokens and each token is looked up as an embedding vector. This part is covered in the Transformers map; here it is the baseline other modalities must match.
Older systems used convolutional neural networks (CNNs) such as ResNet to summarise an image into a feature vector. CNNs build in the idea that nearby pixels matter together.

A ViT, introduced in 2020, cuts the image into a grid of patches, flattens each patch, maps it to a vector with one matrix multiply, and feeds the sequence to a transformer encoder as if the patches were words.

manas.q: How does a vision transformer read an image?

children.note: A 224×224 image cut into 16×16 patches gives (224/16)² = 14 × 14 = 196 patches, so 196 image tokens. Higher resolution means many more tokens and more compute.

manas.q: How many 16×16 patches does a 224×224 image give?

children.note: Like words, patches need position information so the model knows which patch was top-left and which was bottom-right. A learned position vector is added to each patch embedding.
ViTs have fewer built-in assumptions about images, so they tend to need more training data than CNNs, but they scale to very large sizes. Hybrids mixing both are common.

manas.q: Why do ViTs usually need more data than CNNs?

children.note: Sound is a waveform of air-pressure samples. Most speech models first convert it into a spectrogram: a picture of which frequencies are loud over time, often on the mel scale that follows human hearing.

manas.q: What is a spectrogram?

children.note: Because a spectrogram is a 2-D grid (time × frequency), image-style encoders and transformers can process it in chunks, much like patches.
Whisper, released by OpenAI as open-source in September 2022, is an encoder-decoder transformer for speech: the encoder reads the spectrogram and the decoder writes the transcript or a translation.
Neural audio codecs compress sound into a short stream of discrete codes. These codes act like tokens, so a language model can read and also generate speech one code at a time.

manas.q: How can a language model generate speech token by token?

children.note: Video is usually handled as a sample of frames, each encoded like an image, plus timing information. A one-minute clip can produce thousands of tokens, so frames are sampled or compressed.
The same recipe works for depth maps, medical volumes, satellite bands and robot sensor readings: design an encoder that turns the signal into a sequence of vectors.
Contrastive learning puts images and text into one shared space where similar meanings sit close together.

In a joint embedding space a photo of a cow and the caption "a cow in a field" become nearby vectors, while unrelated pairs land far apart. Distance then means difference in meaning across modalities.

manas.q: What does a joint embedding space let you compare?

children.note: CLIP trains two encoders, one for images and one for text, so that matching image-caption pairs get similar vectors. It was trained on about 400 million image-text pairs gathered from the web.

manas.q: How many image-text pairs was CLIP trained on, roughly?

children.note: Take a batch of N images and their N captions. Score all N×N pairs; the N true pairs should score high and the rest low. The model learns by pulling true pairs together and pushing the others apart.

manas.q: What does a contrastive loss reward and punish?

children.note: Similarity s_ij = v_i · w_j / T, where T is a temperature. Apply softmax over each row and column, then cross-entropy against the correct match; average the image-to-text and text-to-image directions (a symmetric loss).

logits = img @ txt.T / T
labels = arange(N)
loss = (ce(logits, labels) + ce(logits.T, labels)) / 2
Every other caption in the batch acts as a wrong answer. Bigger batches give more and harder negatives, which usually makes the learned space sharper.
To classify without task training, write a caption per label such as "a photo of a maize leaf with rust", embed each, and pick the label whose text vector is closest to the image vector.

manas.q: How can CLIP classify images it was never trained to label?

children.note: A joint space lets you search photos with words, or find captions for a photo, by nearest-neighbour lookup. Multimodal retrieval for chat assistants uses the same idea.
Text-image encoders like CLIP were used to guide or condition image generators, and many vision-language models reuse a CLIP-like image encoder.

children.topic: Joining vision to a language model
children.note: How a vision-language model (VLM) lets an LLM "see".
Early captioning used a CNN encoder with an RNN decoder; by 2018 transformers replaced the RNN. Modern VLMs instead attach an image encoder to a large pre-trained LLM that can follow instructions.
Take a trained image encoder E and a trained LLM. Add a small network f so that f(E(image)) has the same size as a word embedding. These outputs act as "image tokens" placed among the text tokens.

manas.q: What does the projector in a VLM do?

children.note: Often the image encoder (and sometimes the LLM) is kept frozen at first while only the projector learns. Then the joined model is fine-tuned on image-text and instruction data.
LLaVA is an open research model that links a CLIP-style image encoder to an open LLM through a small projection layer, then tunes it on visual instruction-following data.
Early fusion mixes embeddings from all modalities into one sequence before the main model, which then predicts from the combined stream. The image-token recipe above is an example.

manas.q: What is early fusion?

children.note: Here each modality is processed on its own first, then merged inside the model. Cross-attention layers let text positions query image features without putting image tokens in the main sequence.

manas.q: How does cross-attention fuse modalities?

children.note: DeepMind's Flamingo (2022) inserted new cross-attention layers into a frozen pre-trained language model so visual information could flow in, and it handled interleaved images and text.

Some models are trained from the start on mixed sequences of text, image and audio tokens rather than bolting an encoder onto a finished LLM. Gemini, announced in December 2023, was described this way.

manas.q: What makes a model "natively" multimodal?

children.note: Bolting on is cheap and reuses strong parts, but the LLM learned language before seeing pictures. Native training can align modalities more deeply but costs far more data and compute.
Each image can add hundreds or thousands of tokens, which eats the context window and raises cost. Models compress, crop or tile images to balance detail and price.
To output pictures, a model either emits image tokens decoded back to pixels or hands a prompt to a separate image generator such as a diffusion model.
Hearing, talking and watching.

The classic voice assistant chains three models: speech recognition turns audio into text, an LLM answers, and text-to-speech reads it out. Simple and modular, but each hop adds delay and loses tone of voice.

manas.q: What are the three stages of a cascade voice assistant?

children.note: Newer systems take audio tokens in and produce audio tokens out in one model, so they can respond faster and keep cues like emotion or interruptions. GPT-4o (May 2024) was one example that handled text, images and audio.
Live conversation needs low delay, handling of people talking over the model, background noise and many accents and languages. Swahili, Hindi and other languages often have less training audio.
Speech recognisers can invent words, especially in silence or noise. Whisper is known to hallucinate at times, so check transcripts used for records or medicine.
A video model samples frames, encodes them and reasons over time to answer questions like "when did the goal happen?". Long videos strain context length, so key frames are picked.
Many models describe single frames well but struggle with order, speed, cause and effect, or events between sampled frames.
Real uses, each with its limits.
VLMs can read scanned forms, receipts, tables and charts and answer questions about them. Numbers pulled from images should be checked against the source.

Describing photos, signs and screens for blind or low-vision users, and live captions for deaf users, are among the most helpful uses. Descriptions can still be wrong, so they support rather than replace human help.

manas.q: Name one accessibility use of multimodal AI.

children.note: A farmer can photograph a sick leaf and ask what it might be. The answer is a hint to confirm with an extension officer, not a diagnosis.
Research models read retinal photos, chest X-rays and skin images and draft reports. They need clinical validation, regulatory approval and a doctor in the loop before any real-patient use.

manas.q: Why must medical VLMs stay under clinician oversight?

children.note: A Nature Communications study aligned a pre-trained vision transformer with a Llama-2 language model to build an interactive dermatology assistant; a research system, not a cleared product.
A 2025 paper proposed a test of how often vision-language models invent findings on medical images, showing hallucination is a real clinical risk.
A vision-language-action (VLA) model takes camera images plus a text instruction and outputs robot actions. Google DeepMind's RT-2 (July 2023) pioneered the idea by fine-tuning a VLM on robot data.

manas.q: What does a vision-language-action model output?

children.note: Agents that read screenshots can click and type in apps. Mistakes here act in the real world, so they need careful permissions.
How we measure these models, and how they go wrong.

MMMU (released November 2023) has about 11,500 college-level questions with images such as charts, maps, diagrams and chemical structures across 30 subjects. At release the best models scored around 56%, below human experts.

manas.q: What does the MMMU benchmark test?

children.note: Benchmarks also cover visual question answering, OCR and document reading, chart reading, and hallucination checks. Each covers a narrow slice of skill.
Scores can rise from training-data contamination, multiple-choice guessing, or models answering from the text alone without truly looking at the image. Test on your own real examples.

manas.q: Why can a high multimodal benchmark score mislead?

children.note: A VLM may describe objects, text or people that are not in the picture, often with confidence. Ask it to point to where it sees something, and verify.

manas.q: What is visual hallucination?

children.note: Small print, handwriting, low light and unusual scripts cause misread digits and words. A wrong digit in a dose or amount is a serious error.
Models often miscount objects or confuse left and right, above and below, because encoders compress the image and lose exact layout.
Text written inside an image can fool a model; a label saying "iPod" on an apple once misled CLIP. Hidden instructions in images can also act as prompt injection.
Image-text pairs scraped from the web carry stereotypes and under-represent many regions, skin tones and languages, so outputs can be skewed or unfair.

manas.q: Where does bias in CLIP-style models come from?

children.note: Photos can reveal faces, homes, documents and GPS location in metadata; voice recordings can identify a person. Get consent, strip metadata and follow local data-protection law such as Kenya's, checking the current text.

nodeData.topic: AI and robots in the physical world
nodeData.note: Robots must sense a messy world, decide and move safely in real time. This map goes from why that is hard, through perception, control and learning, to new robot foundation models, self-driving cars, African drone delivery, humanoids and honest limits.

children.note: A robot must turn messy sensor readings into safe physical movement, in real time, in a world that keeps changing. Mistakes cost broken parts or injuries, not just a wrong answer on a screen.
A machine that senses its surroundings, decides what to do and acts on the world. Building one joins four parts: a power source, a mechanical body, control electronics and software.

manas.q: What four parts does building a robot usually combine?

children.note: The classic recipe: sense (read the sensors), plan (update a model of the world and choose the next move), act (drive the motors), then repeat. It was the main way robots were controlled until the mid-1980s.

manas.q: What are the three steps of the sense–plan–act loop?

children.note: Pure planning is slow, so many robots add fast reflexes that react directly to sensors, like stopping when a bumper is hit. Modern systems mix slow deliberate planning with fast reactive layers.

Observed in the 1980s by Hans Moravec and others: computers found chess and exams fairly easy, but the skills of a toddler, like seeing and moving, very hard. 'Easy' human skills were tuned by millions of years of evolution.

manas.q: What does Moravec's paradox say?

children.note: Sensors drift, wheels slip, light changes, and objects are never exactly where the model says. A robot must act well despite uncertainty, so it reasons about probabilities, not certainties.
A self-driving car cannot pause to think for ten seconds. Decisions must come in milliseconds, and a heavy, fast machine near people must fail safely when something goes wrong.
Language models learn from text on the whole internet. There is no equally large pile of robot movement data, and collecting it on real machines is slow and expensive.
Before a robot can act it must know where it is and what is around it. Perception turns raw sensor signals into a usable picture of the world.
Cheap and rich in detail: colour, texture, signs and faces. But a single camera does not directly give distance, and it struggles in darkness, glare and rain.
Two cameras a known distance apart can estimate depth by comparing the two images, as our two eyes do. Depth cameras measure distance per pixel at short range.
Light detection and ranging: fire laser pulses and time how long the reflection takes to return. Distance = (speed of light × time) / 2. A spinning lidar builds a 3D point cloud of the scene.

manas.q: How does lidar measure distance?

children.note: Radar sees through fog and measures speed; ultrasonic sensors help with parking. Force and touch sensors tell a robot hand how hard it is gripping.
An inertial measurement unit senses acceleration and turning; wheel and joint encoders count rotation. Together they let a robot estimate its own motion, but small errors build up over time.

Combining sensors so the strengths of one cover the weaknesses of another, such as camera plus lidar plus radar. A Kalman filter is a classic tool: it blends a prediction with a new noisy measurement, weighting each by how much it can be trusted.

manas.q: What does a Kalman filter blend together?

children.note: Deep learning models find and label things in images: people, cars, cups. The robot then needs their 3D position and, for moving things, a guess of where they will go next.
Simultaneous localisation and mapping: building a map of an unknown place while tracking your own position on it. It sounds like chicken-and-egg, but good approximate methods exist.

manas.q: What two jobs does SLAM do at the same time?

children.note: Methods include particle filters, extended Kalman filters and graph-based SLAM, which fixes the whole map when the robot recognises a place it has seen before (a 'loop closure').
Robot vacuum cleaners, warehouse robots, drones, underwater vehicles, planetary rovers and augmented-reality headsets all use forms of SLAM.
Once the robot knows where it is and where it wants to be, it must decide the path and push the motors to follow it smoothly.
Measure, compare with the target, correct, and repeat many times a second. The gap between target and actual value is the error; the controller keeps shrinking it.

manas.q: In feedback control, what is the 'error'?

children.note: A PID controller adds three terms. P pushes in proportion to the current error. I adds up past error to remove a steady offset. D looks at how fast the error is changing to brake before overshooting.

manas.q: What do the P, I and D terms of a PID controller respond to?

children.note: output = Kp·e + Ki·(sum of e over time) + Kd·(rate of change of e). Tuning means choosing the three gains Kp, Ki, Kd; too high gives wobble, too low gives sluggishness.
If the drone sinks below its target height, the controller speeds up the rotors; as it nears the target, the D term eases off so it does not shoot past. This runs hundreds of times a second.
The geometry of joints. Forward kinematics: from joint angles, where is the hand? Inverse kinematics: to put the hand here, what angles do I need? The inverse problem can have many answers or none.
Describe the robot by all its joint values as one point. Planning then becomes finding a path for that point that avoids the regions where the robot would hit something.
Finding a sequence of valid positions from start to goal while avoiding obstacles; also called the piano mover's problem. Output becomes speed and turning commands for the motors.

manas.q: What problem does motion planning solve?

children.note: A* searches a grid for the shortest path using a guess of remaining distance. Sampling planners such as RRT grow a tree of random reachable points, which scales to arms with many joints.
Repeatedly plan a short way ahead using a model of the robot, carry out only the first step, then re-plan with fresh sensor data. Widely used where smooth, constrained motion matters.
Hand-written rules break in messy places, so robots increasingly learn behaviour from data: from people showing them, or from trial and error.
Also called learning from demonstration: the robot learns a task by supervised learning from expert examples, such as a person guiding its arm or driving it by remote control.

manas.q: What is another name for imitation learning?

children.note: The simplest form: record pairs of (what the robot saw, what the expert did) and train a network to copy the action. Like learning to cook by watching, without asking why.
A cloned policy makes a small mistake, lands in a situation the expert never showed, and errors snowball. Fixes include collecting extra demonstrations in those new situations.
The robot tries actions, gets a reward signal, and slowly learns a policy that earns more reward. Powerful, but it can need millions of tries, too many for a real machine.

manas.q: Why is reinforcement learning hard to do on a real robot?

children.note: The reward must say what you really want. A badly chosen reward invites shortcuts the designer did not intend, called reward hacking.
A physics simulator lets thousands of virtual robots practise in parallel, faster than real time, with no broken hardware. The learned policy is then moved to the real robot.
No simulator matches reality exactly: friction, motor delays, lighting and sensor noise differ. A policy that is perfect in simulation can fail on day one in the real world.

manas.q: What is the sim-to-real gap?

children.note: Randomly vary the simulation during training: colours, lighting, masses, friction, delays. The policy learns to cope with a wide range, so the real world looks like just one more variation.

manas.q: How does domain randomisation help with the sim-to-real gap?

children.note: A 2023 Nature paper described Swift, an autonomous racing drone trained with deep RL in simulation plus some real-world data. It raced at the level of human champion pilots using onboard sensors.
In practice, learned parts often sit on top of classic control: a network decides what to do, while a reliable low-level controller makes the motors do it safely.
The newest idea: reuse large models trained on internet images and text, and teach them to output robot actions, so robots can follow plain-language instructions.

A VLA takes a camera image and a text instruction and directly outputs low-level robot actions. It is usually built by fine-tuning a vision-language model on data pairing images and instructions with robot movements.

manas.q: What are the inputs and output of a vision-language-action model?

children.note: Web-trained models already know what a 'banana' or 'the recycling bin' is. Connecting that knowledge to actions lets robots handle objects and wording they never saw in robot training data.
Google DeepMind's RT-2, from July 2023, is credited with pioneering the VLA idea: a vision-language model adapted to control a robot arm end to end, from seeing to acting.

manas.q: Which model, from July 2023, pioneered vision-language-action models?

children.note: Google DeepMind's VLA built on Gemini 2.0, launched in March 2025 with a partner model, Gemini Robotics-ER (embodied reasoning). An on-device version for running locally on robots followed in June 2025.

Google DeepMind's newest VLA, tested on over 200 tasks such as using tongs or tying a bow. In a trial on Mercedes-Benz lines, an Apollo 2 humanoid picked and packed parts with a 96% success rate. These are the company's own figures; it is going to robotics partners, not the public.

manas.q: What is Gemini Robotics 2.5?

children.note: An ER model focuses on understanding space and planning: pointing at objects, judging progress, breaking a task into steps. It can direct a separate action model that moves the robot.
One trick is to write robot motions as numbers turned into tokens, so the same model that predicts words can predict the next movement. Other designs add a separate action decoder.
VLAs are still research-stage: slower than classic controllers, sometimes unreliable on long tasks, and hungry for robot demonstration data. Demos show chosen tasks, not every-day reliability.
Self-driving cars and delivery drones are where robot autonomy meets public roads and skies, including real services in Africa.

SAE International defines six levels from 0 (no automation) to 5 (drives anywhere a human could). Level 2 helps with steering and speed but the driver must watch; at Level 4 the car drives itself only within a set area or conditions.

manas.q: How many SAE levels of driving automation are there, and what is Level 5?

children.note: The conditions a self-driving system is built for: certain streets, weather, speeds, times of day. Outside it, the system should not drive itself.
Waymo began offering driverless taxi rides in 2020, but only in limited areas. So far no system has reached full Level 5 autonomy, able to drive anywhere a human could.
Some carmakers rely mainly on cameras with neural networks; others combine cameras with lidar and radar for direct distance measurement. Both use GPS, maps and AI to decide.
Unusual events cause trouble: road works, police hand signals, animals, matatus stopping suddenly, unmarked roads. Software errors have caused crashes and deaths, so testing and regulation matter.
Delivery drones follow GPS routes and use onboard sensors to keep stable and avoid obstacles. Skies are emptier than roads, which made drones an earlier success for autonomy.
Zipline began delivering blood and medical supplies to rural clinics in Rwanda in October 2016 under a government agreement. Rwanda's hills and poor roads make flying faster than driving.

manas.q: Where and when did Zipline start medical drone delivery?

children.note: Clinic staff place an order; a team packs the item; a fixed-wing drone flies out and drops the package by a small paper parachute, without landing. The drone then returns to base.
A 2022 Lancet Global Health study of 20 health facilities found drone delivery cut blood delivery times and reduced expired, wasted blood units compared with road transport.

manas.q: What did the 2022 Rwanda study find about drone blood delivery?

children.note: Zipline launched in Ghana in April 2019 to supply public health facilities, including vaccines. It now also lists centres in Nigeria, Côte d'Ivoire and Kenya.
In 2022 Zipline announced an agreement to build a distribution centre at Chemelil in Kisumu County. Check current news for how far services have grown.
Robots succeed where the need is clear and the task is narrow: one product, one route type, open skies. Payment and government contracts matter as much as the technology.
Robots come in many shapes. The body should fit the job; human shape is one option, not automatically the best.
The most common robots: fixed arms that weld, paint and assemble in factories. They work in fenced, predictable spaces, repeating precise motions.
Wheeled robots move shelves and boxes in warehouses and hospitals. They use maps, SLAM and simple, safe behaviours.
Four-legged robots can walk on stairs and rough ground where wheels fail. Learned walking policies trained in simulation are now common for them.
A robot shaped roughly like a person: torso, head, two arms, two legs. The idea is that it could use human tools, doors and stairs without changing the building.

manas.q: Why do some designers give robots a human shape?

children.note: Balancing on two legs, using dexterous hands and staying safe near people are all very hard. Hands with many joints and touch sensing remain a major research problem.
Many companies show impressive videos. Ask: was it remote-controlled, sped up, or one good take of many? Is it a paid product doing real work, or a demo? Treat bold timelines as claims, not facts.
Robots act on the physical world, so mistakes can hurt people. Knowing the limits is part of using them well.
Heavy, fast machines near people need speed and force limits, emergency stops and safe failure modes. Zipline's drones, for example, carry a parachute that can deploy if serious faults occur.

manas.q: Name two basic physical safety features of robots near people.

children.note: 'Cobots' are designed to share space with workers, slowing or stopping on contact. Industrial safety standards set how close and how fast they may work.
A robot that works 99 percent of the time may still meet strange situations daily at scale. Rare events are the hardest to test, which is why self-driving took so long.

children.topic: Learned behaviour is hard to verify
children.note: A neural network policy cannot be checked line by line like code. Engineers rely on large tests, simulation and guard-rails around the learned part.
Robots can take dull, dirty and dangerous work but can also displace workers. The effects depend on policy, training and who owns the machines.
Robots and drones carry cameras and collect data about people and places. Use and storage of that data should follow the law, such as Kenya's Data Protection Act; check the current text.
General household help, reliable handling of any object, and fully driverless driving everywhere remain unsolved. Most real deployments are narrow and carefully set up.
